title: Meghalaya's 10-Course Feast Brings Khasi, Garo and Jaintia Flavours to Bengaluru
excerpt: The Tribal Expressions dinner at Tijouri, Radisson Blu Atria opened Seeti In Your City, a 14-event national tour carrying Meghalaya's tribal cuisines to Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata and beyond.
body:
• A 10-course Meghalayan feast in Bengaluru opened 'Tribal Expressions', the first edition of Seeti In Your City, at Tijouri, Radisson Blu Atria on 22 October 2026.
  • The dinner showcased the food cultures of Meghalaya's Khasi, Garo and Jaintia tribes, led by chefs including MasterChef India Season 8 first runner-up Nambie Jessica Marak.
  • The programme is run by Meghalaya Tourism and Meghalayan Age with the Seeti Movement, and spans 14 food events across India from October 2026 to February 2027.
  • After Bengaluru, Seeti In Your City travels to Delhi NCR, Mumbai and Kolkata, while the larger Fire & Feast Festival heads to Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Goa, Mumbai and Gurgaon.

A 10-course Meghalayan feast served in Bengaluru has put one of India's least-travelled cuisines at the centre of the table. The dinner, reviewed as a first-person feature by Hindustan Times, was the opening edition of Tribal Expressions by Seeti In Your City, held at Tijouri, the restaurant at Radisson Blu Atria, Bengaluru, on 22 October 2026.

The evening was an intimate, seated introduction to the indigenous food cultures of Meghalaya's three major tribes — the Khasi, the Garo and the Jaintia — built around traditional ingredients, regional cooking techniques and the stories behind the food, according to Meghalaya Tourism. The Hindustan Times account describes a meal that moved well beyond the familiar shorthand of 'Northeastern food', course by course, and a table that included Priyadarshini Raje Scindia, who has championed the initiative.

"Food is one of the most personal ways to understand a place. In Meghalaya, culinary traditions are closely tied to the land, the communities and the knowledge passed down through generations."

— Priyadarshini Raje Scindia

The cuisine behind the courses

Meghalayan cooking is rice-centred and built on boiling, roasting, smoking and fermentation rather than heavy spicing. Its signature dishes include jadoh, red rice cooked with pork; tungrymbai, a pungent preparation of fermented soybeans with black sesame and pork; dohneiiong, pork cooked with black sesame seeds; and nakham bitchi, a fiery dried-fish soup from the Garo hills served before a meal. Bamboo shoot, perilla seed and black sesame recur across the Khasi, Garo and Jaintia kitchens, giving the cuisine a smoky, earthy profile unlike anything in mainstream Indian restaurant cooking.

That distinctiveness is precisely the point of the tour. The Bengaluru kitchen line-up brought together Meghalayan chefs and culinary practitioners led by Chef Nambie Jessica Marak, first runner-up of MasterChef India Season 8 and the state's cultural and culinary ambassador, alongside Ahmedaki Laloo, Benny Paia Dondor Wankhar, Adonijah Lyngdoh, Reuben Zamal Sooting and Fufu Pamei. Shillong restaurants Rynsan and Shad Skye and traditional cooks from the Mylliem area are also part of the wider showcase programme.

A 14-event national tour

Tribal Expressions is the opening act of a larger push. Meghalaya Tourism and Meghalayan Age, in collaboration with the Seeti Movement, are taking the state's culinary heritage across India from October 2026 to February 2027 through two initiatives totalling 14 food events: the intimate Seeti In Your City dinners and the Fire & Feast Festival, a large-format public festival centred on barbecue, live-fire cooking, music and community.

After Bengaluru, Seeti In Your City travels to Delhi NCR, Mumbai and Kolkata, with further editions planned. Fire & Feast Festival will run in Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Goa, Mumbai and Gurgaon, with pitmasters Christopher Fernandes and Vasco Alvares and restaurateur Rizwan Amlani among those taking part.

"By taking Meghalaya's culinary heritage to cities across India, we are creating a platform for cultural exchange and greater recognition of our indigenous ingredients, traditional knowledge and local talent."

— Dr Vijay Kumar D, Commissioner and Secretary, Department of Tourism, Meghalaya

Why it resonates beyond Bengaluru

For Indian food lovers abroad, Meghalayan cuisine is one of the hardest regional tables to find outside India — Northeastern restaurants remain rare in the US, UK and Gulf diaspora hubs, and ingredients such as tungrymbai and dried nakham fish rarely travel. A state-backed tour that puts traditional cooks, rather than fusion reinterpretations, at the centre is a notable shift: the food is presented as a living tribal heritage, not a novelty course in a pan-Indian tasting menu.

Sid Mewara of The Big Forkers, a partner in the initiative, said the idea is "to take Meghalaya beyond a destination people admire from afar and introduce them to its food, its people and the stories behind both." Readers in India can catch the next editions in Delhi NCR, Mumbai and Kolkata; the full programme runs until February 2027.
